Series::is_gpu¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

bool Series::is_gpu() const noexcept

What It Does¶

Returns true when this Series is not on the CPU — that is, when it lives on any accelerator backend.

The definition is literally the negation of is_cpu:

bool is_gpu() const noexcept { return !is_cpu(); }

so is_cpu() and is_gpu() partition every Series — exactly one is true. For the current backend set (CPU, CUDA, MPS) that makes is_gpu() equivalent to is_cuda() || is_mps(), but the definition is “off CPU”, not “one of these two named accelerators” — any future non-CPU backend would also report is_gpu() == true.

is_gpu() is the backend-agnostic placement test. Use it when the branch is “does this tensor need a host round-trip / can it stay on device”, and the specific accelerator does not change the code. When it does — a CUDA-only or MPS-only path — use is_cuda or is_mps to pin which one.

Like its siblings, is_gpu() reports where this tensor currently is, never whether the machine has an accelerator (that is pluss::platform_available(pluss::pCUDA) / pluss::platform_available(pluss::pMPS)), and it never moves data — to(Platform) does that.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

bool true iff platform() != Platform::CPU.

Gradient¶

Not applicable — is_gpu() returns a plain bool.

Examples¶

Example 1. is_gpu() is exactly !is_cpu() — the two always disagree.

auto x = pluss::series::zeros({2});
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "is_cpu=" << x.is_cpu()
          << "  !is_cpu=" << (!x.is_cpu())
          << "  is_gpu=" << x.is_gpu() << "\n";

Output¶

is_cpu=true  !is_cpu=false  is_gpu=false

Example 2. Move a tensor to an accelerator and is_gpu() flips to true, alongside the specific backend predicate. (Output from an Apple-Silicon host where MPS is available.)

auto x = pluss::series::zeros({2});
auto m = x.to(pluss::pMPS);
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "is_gpu=" << m.is_gpu()
          << " is_cuda=" << m.is_cuda()
          << " is_mps=" << m.is_mps() << "\n";

Output¶

is_gpu=true is_cuda=false is_mps=true

is_gpu() tells you the tensor is off the CPU; is_mps tells you which accelerator it landed on. On a CUDA host the same move to pluss::pCUDA would give is_gpu=true is_cuda=true is_mps=false.

Example 3. is_gpu() is the branch to write when the backend identity does not matter — for example “materialize on the host only if it isn’t already there”.

auto stay_or_fetch = [](const pluss::Series& s) {
  return s.is_gpu() ? s.to(pluss::pCPU) : s;   // no-op when already on CPU
};
auto x = pluss::series::zeros({2});
auto y = stay_or_fetch(x);
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "y.is_cpu()=" << y.is_cpu() << "\n";

Output¶

y.is_cpu()=true

Example 4. An undefined Series reports is_gpu() == false — because platform() defaults to Platform::CPU, which makes is_cpu() true.

pluss::Series undef;
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "defined()=" << undef.defined()
          << " is_cpu=" << undef.is_cpu()
          << " is_gpu=" << undef.is_gpu() << "\n";

Output¶

defined()=false is_cpu=true is_gpu=false

So is_gpu() == false does not by itself mean “safe to use on the host” — check defined() if the tensor might be uninitialized.

Example 5. is_gpu() does not report machine capability — a CPU-only host still has every Series answer false here.

auto x = pluss::series::zeros({2});
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "x.is_gpu()                          = " << x.is_gpu() << "\n"
          << "platform_available(pCUDA) [machine] = " << pluss::platform_available(pluss::pCUDA) << "\n"
          << "platform_available(pMPS)  [machine] = " << pluss::platform_available(pluss::pMPS) << "\n";

Output¶

x.is_gpu()                          = false
platform_available(pCUDA) [machine] = false
platform_available(pMPS)  [machine] = true

x.is_gpu() is false even though this machine can run MPS — because x itself was never moved there.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • is_gpu() is defined as !is_cpu(), not as is_cuda() || is_mps(). They coincide for the current backends, but the meaning is “off CPU”.

  • It does not tell you which accelerator — use is_cuda / is_mps when the backend matters.

  • It does not tell you whether the machine has an accelerator — use pluss::platform_available(p) for that.

  • An undefined Series reports is_gpu() == false. Pair with defined() when that matters.

  • A binary op still requires both operands on the same platform; is_gpu() being true for both does not mean they are on the same accelerator.

Summary¶

is_gpu() reports whether a Series is on any accelerator:

  • defined as the exact negation of is_cpu — “not on CPU”

  • the backend-agnostic placement branch; use is_cuda / is_mps when the specific backend matters

  • per-tensor placement, not machine capability

  • false for an undefined Series; noexcept, metadata-only

See Also¶

  • Series::is_cpu: the exact complement.

  • Series::is_cuda / Series::is_mps: the strict per-backend tests below is_gpu().

  • Series::platform(): the underlying Platform value (cpu / cuda / mps).

  • Series::to: move a Series between platforms.
